v5.16.2 — MLOps: inference-optimization extension

Closes the gap between MLOps' existing batch-size/instance-tier latency-cost coverage and the narrower, genuinely missing depth around precision, quantization, and serving memory -- without duplicating AI System Design's own scaling, hosted-vs-self-hosted, or token-budget simulators. Two new lessons: "Precision, Quantization, and Serving Memory" (FP32/FP16/BF16/INT8 conceptually, post-training quantization explicitly distinguished from Hugging Face's own QLoRA training-time quantization, KV-cache and context-length memory cost, prefix caching) and "Measuring and Regression-Testing Inference Performance" (TTFT vs. tokens-per-second as genuinely distinct metrics, p50/p95/p99 tail latency, throughput saturation, tail-latency regressions, inference-server concepts named only as vendor-neutral category examples). The existing "Latency, throughput & cost trade-offs in serving" lesson received a minimal, targeted addition naming continuous batching and cost-based model routing as extensions of its own existing batching/instance-tier discussion, explicitly cross-referencing AI System Design rather than re-teaching its scaling or fallback simulators.

Exercises: 18 → 21 (precision-format choice under a stated requirement, KV-cache exhaustion diagnosis, p95-vs-p50 regression interpretation). Quiz: 20 → 23 (precision/quality trade-off, KV-cache memory cost, TTFT vs. tokens-per-second). Projects: 5 → 6 ("Build a Python Inference-Performance Regression Report," no real GPU benchmarking required). Interview prep: 5 → 7. Capstone unchanged, per the approved plan. Estimated hours: 14.0h → 15.5h.

Two new deterministic tasks added directly into the existing MLOps task list (no new interaction pattern needed -- MLOps already used the standard deterministic-simulation style): a Quantization Trade-Off Simulator (FP32/FP16/BF16/INT8, with memory/latency/throughput figures explicitly labeled illustrative, not real vendor benchmarks) and an Inference Performance Regression Analyzer (TTFT, tokens/sec, p95, memory, and quality compared between a fixed baseline and candidate run, correctly distinguishing a regression hiding in one metric from genuine improvement or normal variation). All 6 existing tasks confirmed unchanged and still function correctly alongside the 2 new ones.

No course, route, category, prerequisite, relatedTracks, suggestedNext, path, or roadmap change of any kind -- confirmed directly: MLOps' category (se-core), prerequisites ([]), relatedTracks, and suggestedNext are all byte-for-byte unchanged, and all 54 platform courses remain confirmed at prerequisites: [] with locking still structurally disabled.

A pre-existing test's hardcoded task count was found and corrected, not silently left failing: test_mlops_track.js asserted MLOps' track had exactly 6 tasks -- correctly updated to 8, reflecting this release's intentional addition, not a regression.

Tested: 77/77 script blocks pass Node syntax check (no new JS block was needed -- all additions integrated into the existing MLOps module); the full 56-file jsdom regression suite passes clean, with both new tasks tested via the correct real DOM event (change for selects) through the actual dispatcher; the 14-check theme suite and full 63-route sweep both pass clean with zero regressions; zero duplicate static DOM IDs and zero cross-type ID collisions across all 52 MLOps lesson/exercise/project/task IDs combined; all 6 requested mobile widths confirmed clean in both themes (12 combinations) across all 8 tasks; confirmed no CUDA, required-GPU, or paid-API reference anywhere in the new content.

v5.16.1

v5.16.1 — Hugging Face: practical PEFT/fine-tuning extension

Closes the gap between "I know how to use Trainer" and "I understand how to adapt a model efficiently and evaluate whether it actually helped," without turning Hugging Face into a second deep-learning or LLM course. Two new lessons: "Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning: LoRA and QLoRA" (frozen base parameters, rank/alpha/target modules/dropout conceptually, full FT vs. PEFT, QLoRA as quantized-base training explicitly distinguished from inference-time quantization) and "Preparing and Validating a Fine-Tuning Run," structured into four clearly separated subsections: dataset preparation, training-target construction (label masking and why training on the wrong tokens changes the task), evaluation after adaptation (baseline comparison, catastrophic forgetting, checkpoint selection), and adapter lifecycle (save/load/merge). The existing "Fine-tuning with Trainer" lesson received a minimal, targeted addition -- one clarifying passage on Trainer supporting either full fine-tuning or a PEFT workflow depending on configuration -- not a rewrite. Backpropagation, optimizers, gradient descent, generic tokenization theory, and general model-evaluation methodology are referenced, never re-taught -- confirmed directly by inspecting the new lesson content for these terms.

Exercises: 8 → 11 (PEFT strategy choice under stated constraints, fine-tuning dataset diagnosis, catastrophic-forgetting diagnosis). Quiz: 30 → 34 (full FT vs. PEFT, LoRA rank/alpha, QLoRA vs. inference quantization, catastrophic forgetting). Projects: 3 → 4 ("Design a PEFT Fine-Tuning Plan," no real GPU training required). Interview prep: 6 → 8. Capstone extended (not replaced) with two additional requirements: justifying full FT vs. LoRA vs. QLoRA, and documenting at least one limitation or regression risk of the adapted model. Estimated hours: 15.6h → 18.0h, calculated from the actual new content added, not chosen arbitrarily.

Interactive track modernized, not duplicated: the existing Hugging Face track already used the standard web-track container/layout -- only its individual task-content pattern (a mix of code-editor and multiple-choice tasks) predated the newer deterministic-simulation style used elsewhere on the platform. Rather than bolting on a second, disconnected interaction system, a new mode:'sim' branch was added to the existing task renderer, and three new deterministic tasks were appended directly into the existing task list: a PEFT Strategy Selector (full FT vs. LoRA vs. QLoRA, explicitly not implying a universal best choice), a Fine-Tuning Dataset Inspector (missing responses, invalid role sequences, duplicates, response leakage, all individually diagnosed), and a LoRA Configuration Simulator (rank/alpha/dropout/target-module scope, with every output explicitly labeled "Illustrative / conceptual estimates" and never presented as predicting real training quality or real GPU memory). All 4 existing tasks (1 code-editor, 3 multiple-choice) are confirmed unchanged and still function correctly alongside the 3 new ones in the same nav.

No course, route, category, prerequisite, relatedTracks, suggestedNext, path, or roadmap change of any kind -- confirmed directly: Hugging Face's category (ml-frameworks), prerequisites ([]), relatedTracks, and suggestedNext are all byte-for-byte unchanged, and all 54 platform courses (not just Hugging Face) remain confirmed at prerequisites: [] with locking still structurally disabled.

A pre-existing test's hardcoded task count was found and corrected, not silently left failing: test_final_13_tracks.js asserted Hugging Face's track had exactly 4 tasks -- correctly updated to 7, reflecting this release's intentional addition, not a regression.

v5.16.0

v5.16.0 — LLM Evaluation & Testing (Course 54)

15 lessons covering evaluation as its own engineering discipline: evaluation as evidence for a claim rather than a demo of selected examples, converting vague goals into testable criteria, offline vs. online evaluation, golden datasets, adversarial/edge-case/slice-based evaluation and aggregate-score masking, deterministic and rule-based metrics, semantic similarity and its factuality gap, LLM-as-a-judge failure modes (order sensitivity, verbosity preference, rubric ambiguity), pairwise comparison and counterbalanced ordering, human evaluation and rubric anchors, factuality/faithfulness/groundedness/citation-correctness precisely distinguished, RAG evaluation (retrieval vs. generation failure attribution), agent and safety-critical evaluation (actions and side effects, not just the final answer), prompt/model/pipeline regression testing, and continuous evaluation in production. Existing courses' own narrow evaluation lessons (LLMs, RAG, AI Agents, Prompt Engineering, MLOps, AI System Design, Hugging Face) are referenced throughout, never re-taught -- this course owns the shared methodology.

18 exercises (kept separate from lessons), 20 quiz questions with the locked topic allocation, 5 projects, 5 interview-prep questions, and a capstone requiring at least 3 trade-off justifications, a deliberately refused-as-sufficient metric, a critical slice that must not be hidden, and one scenario concluding "insufficient evidence."

Six interactive tasks, all verified against deterministic Python logic before implementation -- one genuine ordering bug caught and fixed during that verification, not discovered later: the Regression Detector's trade-off branch was initially unreachable because a broader "clear pass" condition matched first, masking the latency-trade-off scenario entirely; fixed by reordering the conditions before any JavaScript was written. The six tasks: an Evaluation-Set Builder that does not reward selecting every case, rewarding coverage instead; a Metric-Selection Simulator correctly rejecting exact-match for subjective or paraphrase-tolerant claims while accepting justified combinations; an LLM-Judge Bias Lab demonstrating order sensitivity, verbosity preference, and rubric-driven inconsistency without ever claiming these controls remove every possible bias; a Pairwise Comparison Tool handling ties, cannot-judge outcomes, and ordering-imbalance warnings; the corrected Regression Detector correctly surfacing a hidden critical-slice regression behind an improved aggregate score; and an Evaluation Dashboard explicitly reporting "no eligible candidate" honestly rather than forcing a winner, with all cost figures labeled illustrative.

v5.15.0

v5.15.0 — Secure AI Applications (Course 53)

15 lessons covering the full approved sequence, centered on the course's core principle: the model may propose an action, but the application decides whether it is valid, authorized, and safe. Covers the AI-specific attack surface, threat modeling, direct and indirect prompt injection, jailbreaks vs. prompt injection (explicitly distinguished, no bypass recipes), RAG-specific security, trust boundaries in AI architecture, the model-suggests/application-authorizes principle, structured output validation and action gating, least privilege and tool allowlists (extending AI Agents' own concept into enforcement), human approval, sensitive-data and secret leakage (two independent paths: context/output vs. logging/telemetry), denial-of-wallet abuse controls, AI security testing and red teaming (with an honest statement of its limitations), and a closing lesson applying Observability's principles specifically to AI-security signals.

18 exercises (kept separate from lessons), 20 quiz questions with the locked topic allocation, 5 projects, 5 interview-prep questions, and a capstone requiring at least 3 trade-off justifications, one residual risk, and one scenario where the system correctly refuses to act.

Six interactive tasks, all verified against deterministic Python logic before implementation: a Prompt-Injection Defense Lab confirming delimiters/labeling alone remain only "partially defended" and require an authorization gate plus tool allowlist to reach "defended"; a Least-Privilege Simulator distinguishing missing, unnecessary, and dangerous general-purpose capabilities; a Trust-Boundary Mapper supporting multiple independent properties per edge (not one exclusive label); an Output Validation/Action Gate correctly sequencing parse, schema, range, ownership, and authorization checks with fail-closed behavior; a Sensitive-Data Leakage Simulator treating context and logging policy as two independent, separately-failing dimensions; and an Incident Diagnosis task where only indirect prompt injection fits all three pieces of given evidence.

v5.12.0 — Influencing Without Authority for Engineers (Course 50)

v5.10.1 — MLOps Model Canary Rollout task corrected: the original design was too shallow to actually demonstrate a canary decision

v5.9.1

v5.9.1 — CI/CD interaction fix: two simulations were broken through real usage despite passing direct function-call tests

The actual bug, confirmed before fixing anything: the cache-speedup and rollback simulators' buttons used data-act="cicdCacheRun(false)" / cicdDeployVersion(true) -- but the platform's dispatcher only converts numeric dispatcher arguments, not booleans, so both false and true arrived as the non-empty strings "false"/"true", which are both truthy in JavaScript. In practice: the "cold cache" button behaved identically to "warm cache" (both showed 5 seconds), and "Deploy next version (code only)" was incorrectly recorded as a schema-changing deploy, triggering the rollback warning even when no schema change occurred. This is the same category of defect caught and fixed in the Distributed Systems circuit breaker (v5.7.1) -- confirmed here through real .click() calls, which the original test suite hadn't used for these two tasks.

Fixed at the dispatcher-argument level, exactly as specified: both buttons now use numeric arguments (cicdCacheRun(0)/cicdCacheRun(1), cicdDeployVersion(0)/cicdDeployVersion(1)), and both functions normalize with Number(arg) === 1 -- verified this correctly handles the dispatcher's string arguments AND real booleans from direct calls (since Number(true) === 1 and Number(false) === 1 evaluate exactly as needed), so no other call site was put at risk.

Verified genuinely fixed through real button clicks, not just direct function calls: clicking "cold cache" now correctly shows 120 seconds and "warm cache" shows 5 seconds; clicking "Deploy next version (code only)" then rolling back now correctly shows the safe message, while "with schema change" correctly triggers the WARNING -- confirmed for both, distinctly, through the actual DOM click path.

Four new regression tests added using real .click() calls (not direct function calls) specifically to catch this exact class of dispatcher-argument bug going forward, matching the pattern already established for the Distributed Systems circuit breaker's own regression coverage.

Nothing else changed: course count remains 47, route count remains 56, all other content, lessons, and the remaining 4 CI/CD tasks are untouched.

v5.7.1

v5.7.1 — Distributed Systems simulation correctness fixes, an honest correction to the v5.7.0 verification claim

The circuit breaker's consecutive-failure counter was not reset on success while CLOSED -- confirmed directly: F, F, S, F incorrectly opened the circuit, since the earlier two failures were never cleared by the intervening success. Fixed so any success resets the counter to zero, matching the label "consecutive failures" honestly. All 5 required sequences (F,F,S,F → CLOSED/1; F,F,F → OPEN; F,F,F+cooldown+S → CLOSED/0; F,F,F+cooldown+F → OPEN with cooldown restarted; a rejected call during OPEN not incrementing the counter) verified against real button clicks, not just direct function calls.

A second, more serious bug found while verifying the fix through actual keyboard/click interaction, not caught by the original functional test: the "Send failing call" and "Send succeeding call" buttons passed unquoted false/true through data-act, which the platform's argument parser only converts to numbers, not booleans -- meaning both buttons silently received the truthy STRING "false"/"true", so the "failing call" button never actually simulated a failure at all. The original jsdom test missed this entirely because it called dsCbCall() directly, bypassing the exact dispatcher mechanism that was broken. Fixed by passing quoted string arguments and converting explicitly inside the function. Reverified via real clicks and real keyboard Enter-activation, not direct calls.

The consistent-hashing simulation's hardcoded "a minority, not all" claim was removed. It could previously show results like "4 of 8 keys moved" (exactly half) while still claiming a minority. Replaced with a genuine classification function (no moved / a minority / half / a majority / all keys moved) driven by the actual computed percentage, verified across all 5 boundary cases.

The hash function itself had a real precision bug, found and fixed: the JS implementation used plain multiplication (h * 16777619) rather than 32-bit integer multiplication, silently losing precision above JS's safe-integer range and diverging from genuine FNV-1a for every single test key checked. Fixed with Math.imul, and verified exact parity against a Python reference implementation using equivalent 32-bit arithmetic -- both produce identical hash positions and identical per-key node assignments for every tested key.

The simulation itself upgraded to a 100-key sample with 15 virtual positions per physical node (rather than 8 keys and no virtual nodes), now showing previous/new node count, the exact number and percentage of keys moved, and an explicitly-labeled approximate expected share with an honest warning that small samples can deviate substantially -- rather than a single overconfident claim.

The unfinished maintainer comment fragment was completed into clear, complete sentences, without introducing another hardcoded course count that would go stale again.

This entry is itself the honest correction to v5.7.0's verification claim: v5.7.0's changelog stated all six simulations were verified before shipping. Independent review found two of them were not fully correct despite that verification, and a third defect (the keyboard-activation bug) was only found during THIS release's own re-verification. That history is not rewritten -- v5.7.0's entry remains as originally written, and this entry documents what was actually wrong and fixed.

Verified unchanged: 45 courses, 54 routes, 2 Company Paths, the Computer Engineering Path still 4 available/3 planned, all 15 lessons/21 quiz/18 exercises/5 projects/1 capstone in Distributed Systems intact, zero duplicate IDs.

v5.5.3

v5.5.3 — Global search fixed: it was still indexing Python, SQL, and OOP's removed course-level exercises, and clicking a result opened a blank panel

The actual bug, confirmed in the delivered file before fixing anything: runSearch indexed every course's coursedata.exercises array unconditionally -- for Python, SQL, and OOP, that array is stale (their real exercises live in the shared bank now), so search still surfaced removed titles like "Sum a list," "Top 5 by price," and "Point class." Every result routed through gsJumpCourse(id,'exercises'), which called cxTab('exercises') on a course with no such tab -- leaving every panel inactive and the screen blank.

Fixed at the data source, not by hardcoding the five known titles: excluded Python/SQL/OOP from the stale coursedata.exercises indexing entirely, and added real indexing of their actual live systems -- Python and OOP search the shared EXALL bank (OOP filtered to its own OOP_EXERCISE_IDS, exactly mirroring what renderExercises already excludes), and SQL searches its real BANK data. Each indexed item carries its own explicit navigation action computed at index time, rather than the render step guessing one destination for every course.

A new shared navigation helper, gsJumpToExercise(track, cardId), replaces the removed-tab destination for these three: closes the search overlay, opens the real registered track, explicitly triggers OOP's boot function first (idempotent, safe on repeat), locates the actual rendered card by its real DOM ID, scrolls it into view, moves focus to a meaningful control inside it (the editor or Check button), and applies the platform's existing reduced-motion-aware highlight class rather than inventing a new animation. It never calls cxTab('exercises') for these three courses.

Tested exactly as specified: all 5 stale queries (Sum a list, Top 5 by price, Point class, BankAccount, Shape hierarchy) checked directly against the fixed search -- four produce zero results (the exact stale exercise genuinely no longer exists under that title), and "BankAccount" correctly surfaces one legitimate live match (OOP's migrated exercise, which genuinely mentions that class name in its own prompt) with the correct new action, never the removed tab. Six genuine live exercises (Python: a standard and a debugging exercise; SQL: a runnable query and a reasoning question; OOP: a runnable and a reasoning exercise) all confirmed searchable, and clicking through confirmed the correct track opens, the real card exists, focus lands inside it on the textarea, and exactly one top-level screen is visible -- for all three systems, not just one.

A defensive cxTab safeguard added, addressing the underlying blank-panel risk directly: if the requested tab has no rendered panel in the current course, it now falls back to the currently active valid tab, or Overview, instead of deactivating every panel. Verified directly: calling cxTab('exercises') on Python now correctly lands on Overview with exactly one active panel, not zero.

v5.4.6

v5.4.6 — A real, longstanding layout bug fixed: Python, SQL, and OOP opened to what looked like a blank screen

Confirmed root cause: the CSS rules controlling the sidebar-plus-content layout for these three tracks were written as .py-app .app{display:flex;...} and .sql-app .app{display:flex;...} -- a descendant selector (with a space), which only matches an .app element nested INSIDE a .py-app/.sql-app element. The real HTML has both classes on the SAME element (class="app py-app"), so this rule never actually matched, and the flex layout it was supposed to apply never activated. Without it, the sidebar and main content stacked vertically instead of side-by-side -- and since the sidebar's height happened to match the full viewport height, the main lesson content was pushed roughly 900px below the fold, appearing as a solid blank/dark screen until scrolled past.

This predates this entire session's work -- confirmed by checking when these specific CSS rules were introduced relative to everything built in this conversation; it's a genuine, longstanding bug in the original reference-standard tracks, not something introduced by any prior release.

Fixed by correcting the selector to .py-app.app / .sql-app.app (no space -- a compound selector matching both classes on the same element, which is what the HTML actually has) for both the base rule and its responsive mobile-breakpoint counterpart. Confirmed OOP was affected too, since it reuses the same .py-app styling. Searched the entire file for any other track using this same broken pattern -- none found; this was isolated to exactly these two rules.

Verified directly, not assumed: before the fix, the main content area's actual rendered top position was confirmed at 908px from the viewport top (requiring real scrolling to see anything) across all three tracks. After the fix, confirmed the sidebar and main content both start at the top of the viewport and sit side-by-side, with display: flex now genuinely applying. Retested at 320/375/768/1440px widths for all three tracks -- zero horizontal overflow anywhere, confirming the mobile-breakpoint fix didn't introduce a new problem.

A second, genuinely separate blank-screen cause found and fixed in this same release: the CSS fix above addresses a fresh page load, but reloading (or navigating back/forward) while scrolled deep into a track's long single-page layout triggered the BROWSER's own native scroll restoration, which jumps back to that same deep scroll position on reload -- independent of any of this platform's own JS. Confirmed by directly reproducing it: scrolling to 30,000px into the Python track, then reloading, left the page at ~30,000px afterward, landing mid-lesson with no heading nearby -- visually indistinguishable from a genuinely blank screen. Fixed with history.scrollRestoration = 'manual', set as early as possible in the page's script, applied platform-wide rather than only to Python. Verified the exact reproduction scenario now lands at scroll position 0 after reload, and separately confirmed the same fix holds for Python, SQL, DSA, Computer Networks, and Computer Architecture -- five different tracks, not just one.

Tested (both fixes): 67/67 script blocks pass Node syntax check; the full 43-file jsdom regression suite passes clean; the 14-check real-browser theme suite passes clean; a full 53-route sweep confirms zero regressions.

Verified in a real browser by calling it for all 9 Full-Stack Path stages individually -- every one now lands on its actual track container, confirmed by checking each container's real visibility, not just that a function ran without error.

New course added: "Digital Systems & Computer Hardware" -- practical and computer-engineering focused, explicitly not a Linear Circuits or electrical-engineering theory course. 15 lessons (transistors as switches, real digital signals, gates, combinational/sequential hardware, memory, datapaths, a tiny processor, hardware interfaces, hardware debugging), 18 quiz questions, 18 exercises kept in their own section, 6 projects, and a "Build and Explain a Tiny Computer" capstone. v5.4.0 — New course: Computer Networks (Course 1 of the Computer Engineering expansion)

Inspected the existing Computer Architecture & Operating Systems course first, as instructed, to confirm no overlap before writing anything -- confirmed it covers CPU/memory/OS internals with zero networking content, so this course fills a genuinely separate gap.

12 lessons covering the requested topic list, grouped into coherent conceptual units rather than one lesson per bullet point: how networks work (LAN/WAN/topologies), network devices, the OSI & TCP/IP models, MAC/IP addressing (IPv4/IPv6/public/private), subnetting explained by PURPOSE only (explicitly no subnet-mask arithmetic, per the exclusion list), ports/sockets/TCP/UDP, the TCP handshake and packet/frame/segment terminology, DNS/DHCP/ARP/ICMP, HTTP/HTTPS/TLS, routing/switching/NAT, firewalls/proxies/load balancers/CDNs, and WebSockets/SSE plus the standard troubleshooting command toolkit (ping, traceroute, dig, curl, netstat).

30 quiz questions, 5 exercises (kept separate from lesson text, not embedded in it), 3 projects, 5 interview-prep Q&As, and a capstone -- "Backend Network Diagnostic Tool," matching the exact capstone concept requested: given simulated DNS/TCP/HTTP/latency signals, identify the likely root cause.

A real 5-task interactive track, reusing the exact same shared Python runtime as every other track (no new runtime introduced): resolving a DNS CNAME chain to its final IP, simulating the TCP 3-way handshake as an explicit state machine, classifying an IP as private/loopback/public without any mask arithmetic, identifying a well-known service from a port number, and the diagnostic-tool logic itself (DNS → TCP → HTTP status → latency, checked in that order, mirroring how a real engineer would actually narrow down a connectivity problem layer by layer). Every solution and starter was verified against real Python, extracted directly from the file's own stored data, not just written and assumed correct.

No Boolean algebra, truth tables, or math-heavy content anywhere -- subnetting is explained entirely through its purpose (isolation, security, organization) with a worked conceptual example, never through mask arithmetic.

Verification performed exactly as required before reporting completion: JavaScript syntax checked (62/62 new blocks, 61/61 pre-existing unaffected); every new code block and every starter/solution pair run against real Python; every referenced function (getPy, RUN_HARNESS, trackNumBadge, trackMentalModel, trackEditorShell, escapeHtml) confirmed to already exist rather than assumed; a full duplicate-ID scan across every exercise, lesson, and project ID in all 43 courses found zero collisions; every interactive button (Run tests, Reset, Mark solved, Hint 1-3, Reveal Solution, Next/Previous) tested; the complete 35-file jsdom regression suite run clean; both dark and light themes tested with real computed styles in an actual browser (not just CSS inspection) confirming correct background/text colors in both directions with zero JS errors; and the existing progress-storage key scheme (net_done_/net_code_) confirmed to be a new, non-colliding namespace, distinct from every other track's own keys.

Precise counts added this version: 1 course, 12 lessons, 30 quiz questions, 5 exercises, 3 projects, 5 interactive tasks (each with its own 2-4 test cases), 1 capstone, 5 interview-prep Q&As, 3 industry-usage examples. Zero existing lessons, courses, or paths modified or damaged -- confirmed via the full regression suite passing unchanged for every pre-existing track.

v3.1.0 — A critical, widespread light-mode contrast bug found and fixed: core lesson and quiz text across all 41 courses

The most serious finding of the entire theme-verification effort: continuing the hardcoded-color sweep flagged as outstanding after v2.0.0, real-browser contrast testing found that the MAIN LESSON TEXT (.cx-lesson-explain) and QUIZ OPTION TEXT (.cx-opt) used by all 41 original courses -- not just the new tracks -- were essentially invisible in light mode: 1.64:1 and 1.24:1 contrast ratios, far below the 4.5:1 WCAG minimum. Every course's lesson tab and quiz tab were affected.

Root cause: these shared classes had light, dark-theme-appropriate text colors hardcoded directly, with no light-mode override -- from before this session's theme work began. Fixed by adding proper light-mode text colors (matching the platform's established light palette) across every affected class: lesson/hint/reveal/project text, quiz options (including correct/wrong states), and the related Code Review Assistant and global-search overlay components that share the same pattern.

Also fixed in this pass: the hub/landing page's own banner headings, eyebrow text, and secondary text (as low as 1.13:1 -- the main course-banner titles were nearly invisible); the shared success/error status colors used by agent-feedback, api-response-box, dsa-testrow, and cx-pm-out across every track (1.41:1 before, now 4.76:1/5.38:1).

One override caught and reverted before shipping: initially added a light-mode override for a badge that turned out to already be self-contained (solid dark background + light text, unaffected by page theme) -- verified the override would have actually made its contrast WORSE (7.6:1 → 1.69:1) and removed it. Not every hardcoded color is a bug; this is exactly why each one needs real verification, not a blanket rule.

Verified via real browser (Chrome for Testing 131.0.6778.204, headless via puppeteer-core), not assumed: re-ran the exact contrast measurements after each fix, confirming genuine before/after improvement with real composited colors, not the platform's own naive alpha-ignoring test artifact (also identified and worked around during this pass).

v3.0.0

v3.0.0 — 41 of 41 courses now have a full interactive track. The audit is complete.

13 final courses built and shipped in this pass: Computer Vision (grayscale conversion, brightness clamping, IoU for object detection, plus CNN/augmentation/overfitting scenarios), NLP (tokenization, word frequency, stopword removal, plus stemming/embeddings/bag-of-words scenarios), Transformers (softmax, scaled dot-product attention, plus why-attention and positional-encoding scenarios), Generative AI (approach-selection, hallucination, prompting-vs-fine-tuning, data-provenance scenarios), GANs (generator/discriminator roles, mode collapse, a real discriminator-confidence calculation, GAN-vs-alternatives trade-off), VAEs (latent space, the reconstruction/KL trade-off calculation, the beta effect, VAE-vs-GAN trade-off), Diffusion Models (the forward process, a real noise-schedule calculation, why diffusion trains more stably, the real sampling-speed cost), Prompt Engineering (a real few-shot-prompt-building function, specificity, chain-of-thought, prompt injection awareness), PyTorch (broadcasting rules, flattened-tensor-size calculation, autograd, CPU/GPU device mismatches), TensorFlow (convolution output-size and parameter-count calculations, eager vs. graph mode, tf.data pipeline performance), Hugging Face (a real pipeline-selection function, model cards, tokenizer mismatches, zero-shot vs. fine-tuning), Resume Prep (quantified impact, tailoring, project selection, length), and Company Prep (research depth, culture-fit signals, which questions to ask, recognizing real red flags).

A real vacuous-pass bug caught and fixed during this pass: the PyTorch broadcasting task's second test case expected None -- which an entirely unimplemented function also returns by default, so it would have trivially "passed" without any real implementation. Caught by testing the unsolved starter against its own checks (the same discipline that caught two earlier vacuous-pass bugs), fixed by adding a genuine third test case with a real, non-None expected value.

v2.0.0

v2.0.0 — Global light/dark theme system, and a critical pre-existing bug fixed in the process

A serious, previously-undetected bug found during investigation, unrelated to this feature request: every one of the 27+ tracks built across this entire session used CSS variables (--sub, --ink, --line, --panel2) that were never actually defined anywhere for the .web-app class they all share. Verified directly via computed-style inspection: text color and borders were resolving to nothing (literally the unresolved string "var(--sub)"), not the intended dark theme. This had gone undetected because jsdom's automated tests throughout this project checked structural things (display:none/block, classes, text content) which don't depend on custom-property resolution -- the color values themselves were never actually verified until now.

Fixed as part of building the requested theme system: defined the missing variables directly on .web-app (dark defaults, matching the same values already proven correct in the platform's original .cx-app hub styling, for visual consistency) -- this alone repairs the bug across all 27+ tracks immediately.

Global theme toggle added on top of that same fix: one shared body[data-theme] attribute drives both .web-app (every track built this session) and .cx-app (the course catalog/hub) simultaneously -- a single toggle, not per-track duplication. A fixed-position toggle button is present on every page load, persists the choice to localStorage, and is unaffected by which course or track is currently open. The pre-existing, independent .py-app-only toggle (built earlier, already working) was left completely untouched.

A genuine testing limitation surfaced and handled honestly: jsdom does not resolve CSS custom properties in computed styles at all -- confirmed via an isolated, minimal test case unrelated to this platform, which failed identically. This means the ACTUAL rendered colors cannot be automatically verified here. What COULD be verified, and was: the CSS rules themselves exist correctly in the stylesheet (checked via the CSSOM directly, not computed style), the dark and light values are genuinely different for the same property, and the toggle mechanics (button, attribute, persistence) all function correctly end-to-end.

Tested: 47/47 script blocks pass Node syntax check; toggle mechanics and CSS rule existence verified via the CSSOM; full 32-suite regression clean (one transient timing flake under heavy load, confirmed to pass cleanly in isolation).

Explicitly not yet done, and now added to the browser-verification list: visually confirming the actual light-mode colors have sufficient contrast and look correct -- this requires a real browser, since jsdom cannot check it. Also not yet done: sweeping the ~600+ remaining hardcoded hex colors scattered across individual components (badges, specific decorative elements) for full theme consistency -- the shared/reused foundation (editors, buttons, panels, nav, hint boxes) is now covered; per-component hardcoded colors are a separate, follow-on pass.

A real bug caught only because the actual commands were executed, not just syntax-checked: two of the simulator's pre-seeded files used doubly-escaped newlines (\\n instead of \n in the JS source), so grep received one giant line containing literal backslash-n characters instead of several real lines -- silently breaking the exact "find only the ERROR lines" task. Node's --check and even the file's own syntax were completely valid; only running the real grep command against the real (broken) file content surfaced it. Fixed, then the full task re-verified end to end: permission-denied correctly fails before the chmod fix, and cat correctly succeeds after it.

v3.12.0

v3.12.0 — The progressive capstone: one Task Tracker app, growing across all 9 Full-Stack Path milestones

One coherent app, not 9 separate projects: a Task Tracker that starts as pure Python logic (M1) and gains a real piece at every milestone -- HTML/CSS/JS interface plus a React (via CDN) rebuild of the same UI (M2), the REST contract it will speak (M3), a FastAPI-style backend with real JWT login (M4, extending the exact JWT functions built in the standalone Backend track), real SQL persistence (M5), version control (M6), containerization (M7), real tests for M1's own logic (M8), and finally deployment guidance (M9). Every milestone includes learning objectives, starter code, an interactive exercise, verification, expected output, and a full solution.

No new runtime anywhere: M1/M4/M8 reuse the shared Pyodide (getPy/RUN_HARNESS); M2 reuses the exact sandboxed-iframe pattern from the Web Development track; M3 reuses the API request/response simulator pattern; M5 reuses the SAME sql.js engine already loaded for SQL Mastery (window.SQL) via a fresh in-memory database, not a second engine; M6 reuses the Git track's fake-repo pattern; M7 reuses the Docker track's structural-check pattern.

A real design flaw caught and fixed before shipping: M8 asks the learner to write their own test functions. Initially, an empty pass-bodied test function would never raise, so it would report "all tests passed" without testing anything -- verified this failure mode existed, then fixed it by parsing the submitted code's AST to confirm each required test function contains an actual assert statement before treating a pass as genuine, re-verified against real Python that empty stubs are now correctly rejected (NO_ASSERT: ...) and real tests still pass.

All non-trivial logic verified against real interpreters before shipping: M1/M4/M8's Python solutions run correctly under real Python; M5's SQL schema and queries verified against Python's built-in sqlite3 (the same dialect sql.js implements) since this sandbox can't load the sql.js WASM engine itself.

M2's React sub-task is honestly labeled: it loads React/ReactDOM/Babel from a CDN inside the preview iframe, which needs the learner's own browser to have internet access (same requirement as the SQL engine elsewhere on this platform) -- flagged directly in the UI, not silently assumed to work everywhere.

Tested: 35/35 script blocks pass Node syntax check; 15/15 functional checks across all 9 milestones (including the M7 Dockerfile structural checks and the M8 vacuous-stub rejection); full 16-suite regression re-run clean.

Real bug caught while wiring this course, not shipped: Data Science's course-data JSON already contained a pre-existing "linked": null placeholder field elsewhere in its object. My usual method (inserting a new "linked" key near the front) silently failed here, because JSON parsing keeps the LAST occurrence of a duplicate key -- the pre-existing null further down in the object was overriding my inserted value. Caught by directly verifying the parsed JSON value (not just checking the raw text), traced to the duplicate key, and fixed by editing the existing null field in place instead of inserting a new one.

Same bug pre-emptively checked across all 41 courses: a scan found this pre-existing "linked": null placeholder already present on Frontend Development, Docker, Databases, Cloud Computing, Cybersecurity, Computer Vision, NLP, Transformers, Generative AI, GANs, VAEs, Diffusion, Prompt Engineering, PyTorch, TensorFlow, Resume Prep, and Company Prep. Every future course track will use the "edit the existing field" method, not front-insertion, avoiding this failure mode entirely.

Verified NOT to repeat the v3.2.1 bug: hint reveal checked for both the .show class and computed display.

v3.2.1

v3.2.1 — Critical regression fix: Hint/Reveal Solution were silently non-functional platform-wide

Found via: real in-browser testing (this was never actually confirmed working in a browser before this release, despite passing every DOM-level automated check) — confirmed present in the frozen v3.1.1 baseline too, so this predates the practice-environment pilot and was not introduced by it.

Root cause: each exercise's Hint 1/2/3 and Reveal Solution content lives inside an outer wrapper (.cx-reveal) whose CSS defaults to display:none, only becoming visible via a separate .show class (.cx-reveal.show{display:block}). cxRevealHint() correctly toggled each inner hint tier's own display style, but never added/removed .show on the OUTER wrapper — so the whole box stayed permanently hidden regardless of what happened inside it, on every exercise, in every one of the 39 courses that use the shared exercise renderer (Python and SQL were unaffected, since they run on a separate, differently-built interactive track).

Fix: one line added to cxRevealHint() toggling .show on #cxrev_<key> alongside the existing inner-tier logic. No architecture changes, no other files touched.

Why automated testing missed it: jsdom (used for all prior automated checks in this session) does resolve CSS cascade/specificity for computed styles, but the inner hint div's OWN computed display (block) looked correct in isolation; only walking the full ancestor chain and checking the outer wrapper's .show class state exposed the real problem. This was found by asking the person testing to run a sequence of DOM/CSS diagnostic snippets directly in their real browser console (mousedown/mouseup/click tracing, elementFromPoint, getEventListeners, then an ancestor-chain walk of computed styles) after static analysis alone found nothing wrong.

Verified: re-ran the full v3.2.0 regression suite (21/21 script blocks, all jsdom functional + full-page tests) after the fix — no regressions. Directly confirmed via jsdom that the outer wrapper now transitions display:none → display:block (with .show class applied) on a real cxRevealHint() call, matching the exact DOM inspection the person ran in their browser.

Not yet independently re-verified in-browser after this specific fix (the investigation that found it was interactive and ended once the cause was confirmed) — this is the one remaining browser-only check before this build is fully closed out.

v3.1.1

v3.1.1 — Checkpoint 1: runnable-exercise package loading fixed + loop guard

Fixed: the two runnable Data Science exercises (NumPy vectorization, Pandas filter & group) failed with ModuleNotFoundError because the shared runner never loaded Pyodide packages. The generic runner now calls loadPackagesFromImports lazily per run (a no-op when nothing new is needed — already-loaded packages are reused, nothing is preloaded globally) with a visible “Loading required Python packages…” state. If a package isn’t available (e.g. torch), the run proceeds and the normal readable ModuleNotFoundError traceback explains the gap.

Added: an infinite-loop guard in the shared run harness (settrace step cap on the learner’s own frames only, ported from the step visualizer’s pattern) — a 5,000,000-step ceiling that leaves legitimate heavy loops (verified up to 1M iterations) untouched while stopping while True: pass in ~3s with a clear message. Applies to every consumer of the shared runner (Python track, OOP track, Data Science runboxes).

Testing (Node, pyodide 0.26.2 — the exact pinned runtime): ds_ex2 → [2 4 6 8 10]; ds_ex3 → East 120 / West 200; second run loads no packages (1ms); syntax error and unsupported-package error render safely; infinite loop trips the guard; 100k- and 1M-iteration legitimate loops pass. In-browser confirmation on Netlify is the remaining release gate before this earns baseline status.

v3.1 — Stable release. Full Release Audit completed.

All three test suites re-run in full: validate_courses.py (0 errors), regression_check.py (0 errors, 0 warnings), perf_regression_check.py (all 6 invariants). A new permanent check was added to the standing suite this audit: platform-wide quiz-concept coverage (search "Quiz-concept coverage" in regression_check.py) — verifying every one of 992 quiz questions across all 39 courses, not just the ones being actively edited in a given session.

A real, valuable finding from that full sweep: 7 quiz questions across 5 courses untouched by any v3.1 content group (web-dev, backend, capstone, frontend-dev, cloud-computing) had been silently unmatched since Phase 2 — invisible to every per-group check because none of those checks ever covered the whole platform at once. Fixed all 7. This is now a standing, permanent safeguard against the same blind spot recurring.

A subtler finding, investigated properly rather than assumed: an adversarial test question was incorrectly reported as "covered" purely because the concept "is" matched as a substring inside the word "this". Investigated which short concepts were genuine (Linux command names like ls/cd are legitimately short and correctly matched) versus risk-only with zero real coverage value (is, for, def, try, set, key across Python/DSA/Transformers) — removed only the latter, verified 0/992 unmatched held afterward. A full structural fix (word-boundary matching platform-wide) was considered and explicitly deferred, since it would change live hint/Focus-Quiz/Tutor behavior, not just testing.

Full import/export round-trip re-verified, including streak reconstruction, Focus Quiz, Tutor, achievements, and Developer Mode's last-import timestamp — all confirmed exact before/after.

Developer Mode audit: every panel verified (versions, course/content totals, LocalStorage usage, engine status, reference integrity, cache-clearing, diagnostic report download, cold hash-route loading).

Cross-course terminology audit: checked all 6 named example pairs (AI Agent/Agent, LLM/Large Language Model, Dataset/Data Set, Hash Table/Hashtable, API Endpoint/Endpoint, Prompt Engineering/Prompting) plus several additional candidates. Found no genuine inconsistencies — every apparent variation resolved to either a false-positive substring match (e.g. "neural net" was purely matching inside "neural network") or legitimate contextual usage (established shorthand within a course, correct noun-vs-verb distinction, or a proper spell-out-then-abbreviate pattern).

Lesson quality sampling (37 lessons, ~10%, all 7 category groups represented): found a real, quantifiable structural gap — 35 of 349 lessons (all pre-Phase-2 legacy content) were missing objectives and commonMistakes fields that every newer lesson has. Wrote genuine, specific content for all 35 rather than deferring, since these are foundational, heavily-used lessons (Python/SQL/OOP/DSA basics) that deserve the same completeness as newer material.

Broken-link audit: all prerequisites/relatedTracks/suggestedNext (39/39 courses), lesson/course ID uniqueness, and live navigation (prerequisite chips, jump-to-lesson pills, search results, Tutor hint destinations) verified both statically and by actually clicking through them.

Documentation updated: added the quiz-concept coverage invariant and the full v3.1 content-expansion workflow (the repeatable 8-step process used across all 6 groups) to the testing/release doc.

Final release checklist: all 39 courses open cleanly; desktop/mobile verified; fresh, heavy-progress (39/39 at 100%, correctly showing 35 of 43 achievements), and reset profiles all correct; keyboard navigation intact (skip-link first tab stop); no stale branding remains.

Flagging this explicitly per the checkpoint framework: not yet at "investigate" (150-300ms), but the next group's number matters — if it crosses 150ms, caching the concept index (built once, invalidated only when course data changes) rather than recomputing it on every dashboard render is the clear, already-identified fix.
  • HTML size: 1434.6 KB (budget: 1600KB)
  • Regression: PASSED · Performance: PASSED (all 6 runtime invariants)

v3.1 (in progress) — Group 1B: Foundations Curriculum Alignment

Added: 59 new lessons and 24 new exercises across the same 6 Foundations courses (Python, SQL, Git, Linux, Debugging, Problem-Solving), bringing each from 1-3 lessons to 9-12 — within the requested 8-12 range — while preserving every original lesson unchanged in its original position. This closes the gap Group 1's quiz expansion opened: a learner should not be assessed on material the platform never taught.

Validated with real code, not a spot check: built a coverage checker replicating the platform's actual concept-matching algorithm (the same keyword-overlap technique the hint system and Focus Quiz use), and required every one of the 180 quiz questions across all 6 courses to match at least one lesson concept in its own course before considering this done. Started at 117/180 questions with zero coverage; iteratively wrote lessons and refined concept phrasing (several rounds revealed that natural-language quiz phrasing — different verb tenses, quote placement, articles — needed shorter, more robust concept keywords than exact multi-word phrases) until reaching 0/180 unmatched.

Verified end-to-end, not just via the checker: confirmed live that the 3-tier hint system's lesson-matching (which was largely non-functional for these 6 courses before, given how little lesson content existed to match against) now correctly identifies genuinely relevant lessons for exercises in every expanded course.

Testing: all 3 test suites pass; file-size budget raised again (1300KB→1600KB) for this legitimate content growth; performance held steady (mlRender actually improved slightly, 63ms→43ms, within normal variance) comfortably under the 150ms watch threshold.

v3.1 (in progress) — Group 1: Quiz expansion, Foundations category

Honest gap flagged, not fixed here: these 6 courses still have only 1-3 lessons each — a real gap from before Phase 2's course-building groups, separate from the quiz-count gap this pass addressed. Worth a dedicated lesson-expansion pass before pushing these particular courses' quiz counts toward the higher end of the 30-50 target, so quiz breadth and lesson depth grow together rather than the former running ahead of the latter.

v3.0 — Stable release. Phase 3 complete.

Documentation added (architecture, course schema & how to add content, storage & backup/merge rules, hints/review/Focus Quiz/Tutor internals, and a testing & release checklist covering the recurring </script> embedding hazard) — five focused developer-facing documents, delivered alongside the platform rather than embedded in it.

Final release gate, run in full: all 39 courses open without console errors; every My Learning tab (achievements, dashboard, skill tree, planner, recommendations, Focus Quiz, backup) and the Tutor tab render correctly for a fresh user; keyboard path verified (skip-link first tab stop, all interactive elements reachable); mobile (390px) and desktop (1440px) clean across every view including Developer Mode; fresh, heavy-progress, imported, and reset profiles all verified; a full export→clear→restore round-trip confirmed exact; no stale course-count or Phase 1 copy found on inspection; validate_courses.py, regression_check.py, and perf_regression_check.py all pass.

From here, further work is Phase 4, not an extension of Phase 3.

v3.9.1 — Phase 3D.4 (part 1): UI polish, loading feedback & Developer Mode

UI consistency audit: checked border-radius, font-size, and terminology consistency across the platform. Most apparent "inconsistency" (13 border-radius values, ~40 font-size values) turned out to be either legitimate distinct contexts (a thin bar-chart cap vs a card, for instance) or low-value/high-risk to retrofit this late — fixed only the one genuine zero-risk case. Fixed a real, if small, inconsistency: SQL's "Engine still loading" error lacked the clarity of Python's equivalent message; both now read consistently.

Loading feedback: added click-guarding to the three genuinely async operations (Check, Review my code, Get Feedback) so a repeated click during an active operation is ignored, verified with a same-tick synchronous test proving the guard engages before any await yields control.

Added: a hidden Developer Mode page (reachable only via #devmode, never linked from any visible navigation) showing build/schema/regression-suite versions, real content totals, live Python/SQL engine status, reference-integrity checks (duplicate IDs, broken prerequisite/related/suggested-next links), platform-owned LocalStorage usage, and a downloadable diagnostic report — read-only except for an explicit "clear temporary data" action that only ever touches the pre-import backup safety net, never real progress.

A real bug caught while testing Developer Mode, not simulated: loading the platform via a direct #devmode or #mylearning URL on a cold page load silently failed to display anything, because the routing script ran before those track containers (appended later in the document) existed in the DOM yet. Fixed at the root by deferring initial routing until DOMContentLoaded, which protects every current and future track container from this same class of bug, not just the one that happened to be tested. Verified the fix resolves both known-affected routes and confirmed normal tracks are unaffected.

v3.9.0 — Phase 3D.3: Data & Reliability

Added: A new "Backup" tab in My Learning with Export, Import, and Reset. Export downloads only the 10 known platform-owned keys (never a raw localStorage dump), in the exact versioned format specified: format, schemaVersion, appVersion, exportedAt, plus progress/quizAnswers/achievements/preferences sections. Import validates before touching anything — JSON parse, format check, schema-version check (rejecting anything newer than this platform supports), then per-section and per-course validation that drops individually malformed entries with a clear report rather than failing the whole import. A preview shows exactly what would be applied (courses with progress, lessons/exercises/quiz counts, unknown course IDs kept-but-flagged) before anything is written. Merge mode keeps the more-advanced completion state and only fills in quiz answers that don't already exist (never overwrites an existing answer unless Replace is explicitly chosen); the daily activity log (which streaks are computed from) merges by taking the max of each counter per day — never summed, never comparing a precomputed streak number, since none is ever stored. An automatic in-browser backup is taken before every import and before every reset. Reset clears only progress/quiz-history keys, explicitly keeping preferences (theme, planner goals), and requires confirmation.

Testing: verified every failure state requested — invalid JSON, wrong format, missing/future schema version, corrupted individual course entries (good entries survive, bad ones are dropped and reported), unknown course IDs, duplicate/malformed quiz-history entries, empty export, a simulated Phase 1/2-era backup with none of the newer keys, and a simulated interrupted write (the app degrades safely rather than crashing). Most importantly, verified the actual success criterion end-to-end: imported a realistic multi-course backup with quiz history and a 10-day activity streak, applied it, reloaded the page, and confirmed course completion, achievements, the dashboard's streak calculation, Focus Quiz's topic selection, and the Tutor's recommendations all correctly reflected the imported state — not just that the JSON parsed.

v3.8.0 — Phase 3D.2: Performance (measurement-first)

Baseline measured across desktop/mobile viewports and fresh/heavy-progress users (all 39 courses at realistic completion levels): DOM node count stays flat after opening 10 different courses (no accumulation), memory stays flat (~9MB, no leak), LocalStorage read/write is trivial (under 5ms even with ~7KB of real progress data).

A methodology correction worth stating plainly: an initial pass measured search at 48–104ms and some tab-switches at up to 33ms using an external test harness (Playwright automation round-trips). Re-measuring with timestamps taken entirely inside the browser (no cross-process calls inside the timed window) showed the REAL cost of every interactive operation — search, tab-switching, opening a course, the Learning Tutor, Focus Quiz generation, concept-tag statistics, the full 5-panel My Learning dashboard — is under 16ms cold and under 5ms warm, most under 2ms. The earlier numbers were measuring test-automation overhead, not the application. Reporting this correction rather than quietly discarding it, since believing a false hotspot is its own kind of regression.

The one real, measured cost: ~360ms one-time page-parse time at initial load (confirmed via Navigation Timing: responseEnd at ~7ms, domInteractive at ~365ms, with no meaningful network-resource blocking — the gap is the browser parsing 1.16MB of inline HTML/CSS/JS). This is a load-time cost, not a repeated-interaction cost. Per the explicit guidance to prefer low-risk lazy-rendering over splitting course data, and given the SQL/Python static tracks are the most heavily-tested, most-used core of the platform, restructuring their rendering for a one-time sub-half-second gain was considered and declined as not worth the regression risk — stated here rather than silently skipped.

Two justified actions taken: (1) debounced the global search input (120ms) — not fixing a measured slowdown (search was already sub-5ms), but reducing redundant computation during fast typing from one call per keystroke to one call per pause, cheap and explicitly requested. (2) Added a permanent, browser-based performance regression suite (perf_regression_check.py) with generous thresholds, not fragile exact timings: repeated-course-open DOM duplication, cross-course DOM accumulation, tab-cycling growth, search responsiveness, heavy-progress-data responsiveness (all 39 courses at 100%: mlRender 35.9ms, course-open 18.6ms — both comfortably under generous ceilings), and data-act listener-count stability across 60 repeated course opens. All 6 checks pass.

v3.7.0 — Phase 3D.1: Accessibility

Added: A skip-to-content link (the first Tab stop on the page, jumping keyboard users past navigation straight to whichever track is currently visible). Fixed 6 genuinely inaccessible interactive elements found in an audit — roadmap step nodes/titles, prerequisite chips, and skill-tree rows were clickable divs/spans with no keyboard path; all now have proper tabindex and role="button", picked up automatically by the existing delegated Enter/Space handler. Added prefers-reduced-motion support that disables decorative animations (lesson-completion flash, panel fade-in, code-cell pop) while keeping the loading spinner, a functional status indicator. Ran a real WCAG contrast audit across the platform's core color pairs and found one genuine failure: a muted gray (#6b7684) used for small sub-labels and placeholder text fell just short of AA (4.19:1, needs 4.5:1) against the dark UI, and its use as a code-comment color was also a near-miss (4.4:1) against the light SQL-editor background. Fixed both directions correctly — lightened for the dark-UI context, darkened for the light-editor context — and verified both now pass.

Phase 3C complete: full integrity pass

Verified before closing out 3C: (1) every tutor action reads from the shared getLessonContext() object, not separate state logic; (2) no feature is labeled "AI" anywhere in the product — the tab reads "Tutor," not "AI Tutor," and every panel's own copy states plainly it's pattern-based/local/not a model; (3) hints, code review, Focus Quiz, and project feedback each carry explicit confidence labels (Confirmed/Likely/Possible) and clear heuristic-vs-authored framing; (4) the hint-fallback path never calls a lesson example "the solution" — it's explicitly labeled as a stand-in when no solution is authored; (5) imported progress (data with no Phase-3C-era keys) and course reset both verified working; (6) all existing localStorage keys remain compatible, no renames; (7) fresh-user and completed-user states verified correct and distinct; (8) all 39 courses confirmed opening without console errors; (9) mobile (390px) and desktop (1440px) verified clean across every course tab including the new Tutor tab; (10) the embedded-</script> regression safeguard was deliberately re-broken and confirmed to still catch it cleanly, with a clear message, no crash.

v3.6.0 — Phase 3C.5: Project Feedback

Added: A "Get Feedback" box on every project card across all 39 courses. Reuses the 3C.2 pipelines directly rather than new logic: Python submissions run through the real Pyodide execution harness (genuine correctness signal: did it error, did it produce output) plus the same AST-based static analysis, regrouped into Correctness/Completeness/Readability/Modularity/Efficiency/Edge cases. SQL submissions get the same calibrated pattern review; since project submissions aren't bound to a specific database (unlike bite-sized exercises), live execution is honestly skipped in favor of the structural review. Completeness is a new, clearly-labeled heuristic: project descriptions are parsed into checkable clauses and matched against the submission by keyword overlap — always "Possible" confidence, never claimed as verification. Every result ends with one concrete "Next improvement," not a rewrite.

Fixed: caught a real rendering bug during testing — SQL submissions with correctness-bucketed findings produced two separate "Correctness" headers (one hardcoded for the execution note, one from the findings loop). Fixed by merging both into a single section, verified with a live test confirming exactly one "Correctness" header appears.

v3.5.0 — Phase 3C.4: Learning Tutor

Added: A "Tutor" tab on every course page — explicit lesson/exercise selectors (not guessed context) feeding six curated, context-aware sections built entirely from getLessonContext() and real course data: Explain this concept (the selected lesson's real explanation/example), What should I review first (incomplete prerequisites, or concepts tied to real incorrect quiz answers), Help with this exercise (opens the 3C.1 three-tier hints, auto-revealing tier 1), Why was my answer wrong (your actual chosen vs. correct answer, plus the closest concept-matched lesson's real explanation, honestly labeled as matched rather than authored-per-question), Give me a practice plan (unfinished lessons + weak concepts, or an honest "course complete" state suggesting the real next course), and Review my code (opens the 3C.2 reviewer pre-scoped to the selected exercise, only offered when a live editor actually exists). Every section states plainly what real data it drew from.

Testing: verified the requested empty states individually and correctly distinct from each other — no lesson selected, no quiz mistakes yet, no current exercise, prerequisites already complete, and course fully completed (which correctly suggests the course's real suggested-next). Also verified an exercise with no authored solution routes cleanly to the hint flow instead of failing silently, and a fresh user sees only honest gaps, no fabricated guidance.

v3.4.0 — Phase 3C.3: Adaptive Quiz Generator ("Focus Quiz")

Added: A new "Focus Quiz" tab in My Learning that curates and mixes real quiz questions from across all 39 courses by concept, rather than inventing new ones (which would need real generative AI this platform doesn't have). Every quiz question is concept-tagged by real keyword overlap against its course's lesson concepts — the same honest, scalable technique from 3C.1's hint system. Selection mixes ~75% questions from concepts you've recently missed with ~25% spaced review of concepts you've mastered (oldest-practiced first), and always explains why: "This quiz focuses on X because you've missed Y% of recent questions on it," or "You're doing well across the board — this is spaced review to keep it fresh." Works immediately from existing quiz answers (no separate history required to start), and layers in a new timestamped log going forward for real recency-based spaced review, fed by both regular quiz-taking and Focus Quiz sessions alike.

Testing: verified all 9 scenarios requested — new user, mostly correct, mostly incorrect, one weak topic among many strong, multiple weak topics, no quizzes completed, all quizzes completed, reset progress, and imported progress (data with no adaptive history) — each behaves honestly and predictably. Caught and fixed one real bug this way: the "mastered concept" threshold originally required 2+ attempts per concept, which is unrealistic given how fine-grained concept tags are, and caused a "mostly correct" learner to see an empty/exhausted state instead of spaced review. Fixed and re-verified against all 9 scenarios before shipping.

v3.3.0 — Phase 3C.2: Code Review Assistant

Added: A "Review my code" button on every Python exercise (interactive Python track, OOP, and the runnable Data Science exercises) and every SQL exercise. Python review runs a real AST-based static analysis inside the browser's own Python interpreter (Python's own ast module, not a guess) — catches bare/broad except, mutable default arguments, ambiguous single-letter names (l/O/I), non-nested range(len()) loops, mutating a list while iterating it, unused variables, near-duplicate code blocks, missing empty-input handling, and deep nesting. SQL review is a calibrated pattern scan covering SELECT *, WHERE vs HAVING misuse, cartesian-product risk, missing JOIN conditions, NULL comparison mistakes, mixed aggregate/non-aggregate columns without GROUP BY, and readability/aliasing. Every finding carries a confidence label (Confirmed/Likely/Possible) matched to how certain the check actually is, and results are structured into what looks good, the issue, why it matters, and a suggested next step — never a full rewrite.

On false positives: caught and fixed one during testing — the range(len()) check initially flagged legitimate matrix-multiplication code (which genuinely needs index-based cross-referencing across multiple arrays) as "likely" needing enumerate(). Fixed by only flagging non-nested loops and downgrading to "possible," verified against the original test case plus 8 other scenarios (simple correct code, recursion, legitimate nested grids, underscore-convention loop vars) to confirm zero false positives before shipping.

v3.2.0 — Phase 3C.1: Shared context object & 3-tier hints

Important scope note: this platform is a static HTML file with no backend or API keys, so "AI" features in Phase 3C are built as genuinely useful, honestly-labeled rule-based and heuristic systems — not real LLM calls, which would require exposing a secret key client-side or a server this project doesn't have.

Added: getLessonContext() — a single shared context object (course, lesson, concepts, prerequisites, completed lessons/exercises, quiz history, current exercise, language) that every subsequent AI-assistance feature will read from, instead of each maintaining separate state-reading logic. Every exercise across all 39 courses now gets a real 3-tier hint system: Hint 1 (a nudge naming the most relevant lesson and its concepts, matched by real keyword overlap — not hand-tagged, so it works instantly across ~200 exercises), Hint 2 (the exercise's own authored strategy hint where present), Hint 3 (the authored solution where present, or an honest fallback to the matched lesson's own example code with a clear note that no worked solution exists yet for that specific exercise).
