Adaptive tools
SQL Mastery · complete course

From zero to interview-ready — one document

Foundations from first principles, an adaptive practice lab that tracks your weak spots, every advanced topic in MySQL-default + browser format, and two real projects with a portfolio kit. Everything runs live on three real databases in your browser.

Loading engine + building the student & company databases…
How to use this. Read the lessons top to bottom (Foundations → Basics → Advanced), then drill in the Practice Lab — it feeds you questions from every topic at the right difficulty and won't call a topic "mastered" until you're consistently right. The advanced lessons show 🐬 MySQL (the default) and 💜 browser (SQLite) side by side, with orange boxes for the differences. Three databases run here: a small teaching set, a 2,000-student Student DB, and a ~30k-row Nimbus company DB.

1 · What is a database, and why does one exist?

First principlesA database exists to store facts without duplicating them, and answer questions about them quickly and correctly — even at millions of rows with many people reading and writing at once. Every feature you'll learn serves those two goals.
AnalogyRun a shop on one giant spreadsheet: every order re-pastes the customer's full address. Betty orders 40 times → her address sits in 40 cells. She moves → you must fix all 40 and you'll miss some. Two staff edit at once and overwrite each other. That pain — duplicated facts, inconsistent updates, collisions — is exactly what a database removes.

The fix: store each kind of fact once, in its own table, and link with IDs. Betty lives in Customers once; each order stores a small customer_id pointing at her. That's the seed of relational databases.

SQL is the language you use to talk to it. MySQL is one program that speaks SQL (PostgreSQL, SQLite, SQL Server, Oracle are others).

2 · Primary keys & foreign keys

First principlesIf tables link by ID, every row needs a guaranteed-unique ID (primary key), and a link column must point at a real row (foreign key). PK/FK are what make "linking by ID" trustworthy.
AnalogyA primary key is a passport number — unique, never blank, never reused. A foreign key is writing that number on a booking: it references the one passport instead of copying the whole person.
One student → many enrollments (one-to-many). The FK must match a real PK.

Both sides many (students take many courses, courses have many students) = many-to-many, modelled with a bridge table (that's what enrollments is).

3 · How professionals think when writing SQL

MindsetPros start from the question and the shape of the answer, then work back to clauses. Syntax is last.
  1. What's one row of my answer? "per customer" vs "per country" decides GROUP BY.
  2. Which tables hold the columns? Name in Customers, amount in Orders → JOIN.
  3. Filters — row-level (WHERE) or group-level (HAVING)?
  4. Summarize? "per something" → GROUP BY + aggregate.
  5. Order & trim last (ORDER BY / LIMIT).
-- you TYPE:  SELECT → FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY
-- DB RUNS:   FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY
Why it matters: SELECT runs late, so an alias made in SELECT usually can't be used in WHERE. That explains a whole class of errors.
Where this shows up in real backend workThis 'pros think in sets, not loops' mindset shift is exactly what separates a junior engineer's first ORM-heavy code (looping and querying in a for-loop, N+1 style) from a senior engineer's single well-shaped query -- and it's one of the most common code-review comments backend engineers give each other.

4 · How to read someone else's SQL

SkillDon't read top-to-bottom. Read in execution order, FROM first.
  1. Find FROM/JOINs — what's on the table.
  2. Read WHERE — which rows survive.
  3. Spot GROUP BY — answer is per-group.
  4. Now read SELECT — final shape.
  5. Peel subqueries inside-out — each is a temp table.
SELECT c.department, AVG(e.score) AS avg_score
FROM enrollments e JOIN courses c ON e.course_id=c.course_id
WHERE e.semester='2024F' GROUP BY c.department
HAVING AVG(e.score)>75 ORDER BY avg_score DESC;
Narration: "enrollments joined to courses, keep Fall-2024, bucket by department, average scores, keep departments above 75, best first." One breath.
Where this shows up in real backend workReading unfamiliar SQL is a daily task -- inheriting a legacy dashboard query, debugging a slow report someone else wrote, reviewing a teammate's migration. Being able to parse a query you didn't write is as important as writing your own.

5 · What MySQL does inside

Under the hoodFor every query the DB asks: "can I jump straight to the rows, or must I read them all?"

SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE amount > 500; — no index → full table scan (reads every row; cost grows with the table). With an index on amount → it's a sorted B-tree, so the DB jumps to 500 and walks forward, reading only matches. O(n) vs ~O(log n).

See itPut EXPLAIN before any query in Workbench: type=ALL = scan, ref/range = index used, rows = estimated rows read. You'll prove this live in the Indexes lesson.
Trade-off: indexes speed reads but slow writes and cost disk — index foreign keys and common WHERE/JOIN columns, not everything.
Where this shows up in real backend workUnderstanding what MySQL actually does with your query (parse, optimize, execute) is what lets you reason about WHY a query is slow instead of just guessing -- the difference between trial-and-error tuning and targeted fixes.

6 · Dialect differences (what's portable)

TaskMySQLPostgreSQLSQL ServerSQLite
LimitLIMIT 10LIMIT 10TOP 10LIMIT 10
ConcatCONCAT(a,b)a||ba+ba||b
Null fallbackIFNULL/COALESCECOALESCEISNULL/COALESCEIFNULL/COALESCE
Auto idAUTO_INCREMENTSERIALIDENTITYINTEGER PK
Month of dateDATE_FORMAT / MONTH()to_charFORMATstrftime
Full outer join❌ emulate✅✅✅
Portable habit: prefer COALESCE, explicit JOIN ... ON, standard aggregates. This lab is SQLite, so || works here; on MySQL use CONCAT.
Where this shows up in real backend workAny real backend team eventually touches more than one database (MySQL in production, SQLite in tests, Postgres for a new service) -- knowing which SQL is portable and which isn't saves you from a migration surprise.

7 · SELECT & DISTINCT — asking a table for columns

WhySELECT is how you ask a table for specific columns. Everything else — filtering, sorting, joining — is built on top of it. If you can't picture the columns you want, you can't write the query.

These are the small teaching tables the basics run on (they live in the browser lab):

Customers

customer_idfirst_namelast_nameagecountry
1JohnDoe31USA
2RobertLuna22USA
3DavidRobinson22UK
4JohnReinhardt25UK
5BettyDoe28UAE

Orders

order_iditemamountcustomer_id
1Keyboard4004
2Mouse3004
3Monitor120003
4Keyboard4001
5Mousepad2502

Name the columns you want, then the table. * means "all columns"; AS renames a column in the output.

SELECT first_name, age FROM Customers;
SELECT * FROM Customers;                    -- every column
SELECT first_name AS name FROM Customers;   -- rename in output

DISTINCT removes duplicate values — useful when a column repeats:

SELECT DISTINCT country FROM Customers;   -- USA, UK, UAE (each once)

You can also build a new column from existing ones — like joining first and last name. This is the first place MySQL and the browser differ:

🐬 MySQL 
SELECT CONCAT(first_name,' ',last_name) AS full_name
FROM Customers;
💜 Browser (SQLite) 
SELECT first_name || ' ' || last_name AS full_name
FROM Customers;
MySQL vs SQLiteMySQL joins text with CONCAT(a, ' ', b); SQLite (and Postgres) use the || operator. This is one of the very few differences at the beginner level — SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY and GROUP BY are otherwise identical in both.
❌ Missing comma
SELECT first_name age FROM Customers;
SQL reads age as an alias for first_name.
✅ Correct
SELECT first_name, age FROM Customers;
Where this shows up in real backend workSELECT is the first line of almost every read path in a backend service -- fetching a user's profile, a product listing, an order history. DISTINCT specifically shows up constantly in reporting and analytics endpoints.
Step 1 · Explanation

8 · WHERE — filtering rows

WhyWHERE keeps only the rows that pass a test. Without it you get the whole table; with it you get exactly the slice you care about — "just the UK customers", "just orders over 300".
Step 2 · Guided example

The operators: =, != (or <>), >, <, >=, <=, combined with AND, OR, NOT. Then four handy extras:

SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE country = 'USA';
SELECT * FROM Orders    WHERE amount > 300;
SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE country IN ('USA','UAE');       -- a list
SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE age BETWEEN 22 AND 28;         -- inclusive range
SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE first_name LIKE 'J%';         -- pattern: starts with J
SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE country IS NULL;             -- missing value
Two things beginners trip on: text needs single quotes (country = 'USA', not country = USA), and NULL needs IS/IS NOT — never =. In LIKE, % matches any run of characters and _ matches exactly one.
❌ Unquoted text
WHERE country = USA
SQL looks for a column named USA and errors.
✅ Quoted
WHERE country = 'USA'
Step 3 · Practice — easy

Two exercises using exactly the patterns above.

Step 4 · A bit harder

Pattern matching with LIKE — a different mental model than a plain equality check.

Step 5 · Mixed — combines with SELECT DISTINCT

Pulls in DISTINCT from the previous lesson alongside this lesson's WHERE.

Step 6 · Interview-style

Stacking AND with a negation — a common real screening question shape.

Step 7 · Mastery checkpoint
Where this shows up in real backend workEvery API endpoint that filters by a parameter (user_id, status, date range) is a WHERE clause. Getting comfortable here directly maps to writing correct query parameters in a real backend route.

9 · ORDER BY & LIMIT — sorting and trimming

WhyORDER BY sorts the result; LIMIT caps how many rows come back. Together they answer every "top N" question — biggest order, youngest customer, three cheapest items.
SELECT * FROM Customers ORDER BY age;          -- ASC (smallest first) is default
SELECT * FROM Customers ORDER BY age DESC;     -- largest first
SELECT * FROM Customers ORDER BY country, age; -- sort by country, then age within it
SELECT * FROM Orders ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 1;         -- the single biggest
SELECT * FROM Orders ORDER BY amount LIMIT 2 OFFSET 1;      -- skip 1, take next 2
OFFSET skips rows before LIMIT grabs them — that's how "the 2nd and 3rd cheapest" works: sort ascending, OFFSET 1 to skip the cheapest, LIMIT 2 for the next two.
Where this shows up in real backend workPagination (LIMIT/OFFSET) and 'most recent first' feeds are ORDER BY in production disguise -- this is the exact mechanism behind infinite-scroll APIs and admin dashboards.

10 · Aggregate functions — summarizing

WhyAggregates collapse many rows into one summary number. This is the jump from "list the data" to "analyze the data": how many, the total, the average, the biggest.
SELECT COUNT(*)     FROM Customers;   -- how many rows
SELECT SUM(amount)  FROM Orders;      -- grand total
SELECT AVG(age)     FROM Customers;   -- average
SELECT MAX(amount), MIN(amount) FROM Orders;  -- biggest & smallest together
COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column): COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(column) counts only rows where that column isn't NULL. Identical on these tables, but the distinction matters the moment NULLs appear.
Where this shows up in real backend workDashboards and analytics endpoints -- total revenue, average order value, active user counts -- are aggregate functions. This is the backbone of any /stats or /metrics endpoint you'll build.

11 · GROUP BY & HAVING — one result per category

WhyUse GROUP BY whenever you want one result per category instead of one per row — "customers per country", "total per customer". HAVING then filters those groups. That intuition — "per something" means GROUP BY — sticks better than the syntax.
SELECT country, COUNT(*) FROM Customers GROUP BY country;
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM Orders GROUP BY customer_id;
The rule: every column in SELECT must be either in the GROUP BY or wrapped in an aggregate. And the difference that trips everyone up: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after the aggregate is computed.
❌ WHERE on an aggregate
SELECT country, COUNT(*) FROM Customers
WHERE COUNT(*) > 1 GROUP BY country;
✅ HAVING for groups
SELECT country, COUNT(*) FROM Customers
GROUP BY country HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
Where this shows up in real backend workPer-customer totals, per-day counts, per-category breakdowns -- any 'group by X, show me Y' report in a real product is GROUP BY. This is one of the most requested query shapes from product/data teams.

12 · JOINs — combining tables

WhyData is split across tables to avoid duplication (a name in Customers, an amount in Orders). A JOIN stitches them back together on a shared id, so you can show a customer's name next to their order.
AnalogyAn order says "customer #4". The join is you flipping to the Customers page to read who #4 is, and stapling the two facts side by side.

INNER JOIN keeps only rows that match on both sides. A customer with no orders simply won't appear:

SELECT c.first_name, o.item
FROM Customers c
JOIN Orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table, matched or not — unmatched right-side columns come back NULL. That NULL is how you find customers with no orders:

SELECT c.first_name, o.item
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.item IS NULL;   -- the customers who never ordered
Two things: c and o are table aliases so you don't retype full names. And on these teaching tables, the Shippings table links on a column literally named customer (not customer_id) — a classic gotcha when you write that join.
❌ No ON (accidental cross join)
FROM Customers c, Orders o
-- every customer paired with every order
✅ Explicit match
FROM Customers c
JOIN Orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
Where this shows up in real backend workAlmost no real query touches just one table -- fetching an order WITH its customer, a post WITH its author, a ticket WITH its assignee is a JOIN. This is arguably the single most-used SQL skill in backend work.

13 · SQL syntax essentials (MySQL default)

WhyThe six clauses and the order you type them — the backbone every advanced topic hangs off.
🐬 MySQL 
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM products WHERE price>50
GROUP BY category HAVING COUNT(*)>5
ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 10;
💜 Browser (SQLite) 
-- identical
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM products WHERE price>50
GROUP BY category HAVING COUNT(*)>5
ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 10;
MySQL vs SQLiteThe query language is identical. Differences appear only at the edges (strings, dates, DDL, auto-increment) — flagged as each lesson hits them.
Where this shows up in real backend workConsistent query structure and clause ordering is what makes a codebase's SQL reviewable -- a teammate should be able to scan your query and immediately know what it does.

14 · Database design — requirements → tables → constraints

WhyA good schema makes hard questions easy. Design is the most valued SQL interview skill — it shows you understand the data.
AnalogyDesign is laying out a warehouse before stocking it: each type in its own labelled aisle (table), every item a barcode (PK), barcodes on shipping labels (FK) instead of re-describing items.
🐬 MySQL 
CREATE TABLE order_items (
  item_id    INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id   INT NOT NULL,
  product_id INT NOT NULL,
  quantity   INT NOT NULL CHECK(quantity>0),
  unit_price DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
  FOREIGN KEY(order_id)   REFERENCES orders(order_id),
  FOREIGN KEY(product_id) REFERENCES products(product_id)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;
💜 Browser (SQLite) 
CREATE TABLE order_items (
  item_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id   INTEGER NOT NULL,
  product_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  quantity   INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK(quantity>0),
  unit_price REAL NOT NULL,
  FOREIGN KEY(order_id)   REFERENCES orders(order_id),
  FOREIGN KEY(product_id) REFERENCES products(product_id)
);
MySQL vs SQLiteAuto id: MySQL INT AUTO_INCREMENT → SQLite INTEGER PRIMARY KEY. Types: MySQL strict (VARCHAR(n),DECIMAL,DATE); SQLite loose (TEXT,REAL). Engine: ENGINE=InnoDB MySQL-only. FK enforcement: on by default in InnoDB; SQLite needs PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON;.
Each constraint prevents a bug: PRIMARY KEY (no dup/blank ids), FOREIGN KEY (no orphan references), NOT NULL (required), UNIQUE (no duplicate emails), CHECK (quantity>0), DEFAULT (auto-fill). Correctness lives in the DB, immune to app bugs.
💬 Interview — design
  • Primary vs unique key?
    aOne PK per table (identity, NOT NULL); many UNIQUEs allowed, may permit a NULL.
  • Why not store customer name on each order?
    aDuplication → update anomalies. Normalize; reference by id.
  • When denormalize?
    aRead-heavy analytics where joins are too slow — trade duplication for speed, keep copies in sync.
Where this shows up in real backend workSchema design decisions (which table owns which data, how foreign keys relate) made early in a project are expensive to change later -- this is genuinely one of the highest-leverage skills for a backend engineer building something from scratch.

15 · Joins (deep dive)

WhyDesign splits data; joins recombine it for a question. Mastery = fluently walking the foreign-key links.
❌ No ON (cross join)
FROM orders o, order_items oi
WHERE ...  -- millions of rows
✅ JOIN ... ON
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id=oi.order_id
MySQL vs SQLiteJOIN syntax identical. Only FULL OUTER JOIN differs: SQLite has it, MySQL emulates with LEFT ∪ RIGHT.

▶ 3-table join on Nimbus

Where this shows up in real backend workDeeper JOIN patterns (self-joins, multi-table joins) show up in things like org-chart queries (an employee's manager, who is also an employee), or connecting a many-to-many relationship like tags on a post.

16 · Subqueries

WhySome questions need an inner answer first ("above the average"). A subquery computes it and feeds the outer query. Shapes: scalar, IN/NOT IN, EXISTS, derived table.
EXISTS vs IN: IN builds the whole list; EXISTS stops at the first match and handles NULLs more safely than NOT IN.
💬 Interview — subqueries
  • Easy: products never ordered → NOT IN/NOT EXISTS.
  • Medium: 2nd-highest total → MAX below the MAX, or DENSE_RANK()=2.
  • Hard: customers whose every order is completed → NOT EXISTS a non-completed order.
Where this shows up in real backend workSubqueries are how you answer 'compare this row to an aggregate' questions -- 'customers who spent more than average,' 'products priced above their category's median' -- extremely common in real reporting.

17 · CTEs (WITH)

WhyNested subqueries get unreadable. A CTE names an intermediate result and builds on it top-to-bottom — same power, far clearer.
AnalogyA CTE is a labelled prep bowl: chop into "spend_per_customer" once, set aside, then cook using that bowl by name.
🐬 MySQL 
WITH spend AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(oi.quantity*oi.unit_price) AS total
  FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id=oi.order_id
  WHERE o.status='completed' GROUP BY o.customer_id)
SELECT customer_id,total FROM spend
ORDER BY total DESC LIMIT 5;
💜 Browser 
-- identical syntax
WITH spend AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(oi.quantity*oi.unit_price) AS total
  FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id=oi.order_id
  WHERE o.status='completed' GROUP BY o.customer_id)
SELECT customer_id,total FROM spend
ORDER BY total DESC LIMIT 5;
MySQL vs SQLiteCTEs identical (MySQL 8.0+, modern SQLite). Recursive CTEs work in both — for hierarchies (org charts, category trees).
Where this shows up in real backend workCTEs (WITH clauses) are how production SQL stays readable when a query has several logical steps -- most teams' style guides require breaking complex queries into named CTEs specifically for review-ability.

18 · Window functions

WhyGROUP BY collapses rows; window functions compute across rows but keep every row — rankings, running totals, "compare each row to its group." The core of analytics.
AnalogyGROUP BY = "class average" (one number). Window = writing each student's score, the class average, AND their rank next to every student, nobody removed.
🐬 MySQL 
WITH rev AS(
 SELECT DATE_FORMAT(o.order_date,'%Y-%m') AS ym,
        SUM(oi.quantity*oi.unit_price) AS revenue
 FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id=oi.order_id
 WHERE o.status='completed' GROUP BY ym)
SELECT ym,revenue,
  SUM(revenue) OVER(ORDER BY ym) AS running
FROM rev ORDER BY ym;
💜 Browser 
-- only the date fn changes: strftime
WITH rev AS(
 SELECT strftime('%Y-%m',o.order_date) AS ym,
        SUM(oi.quantity*oi.unit_price) AS revenue
 FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id=oi.order_id
 WHERE o.status='completed' GROUP BY ym)
SELECT ym,revenue,
  SUM(revenue) OVER(ORDER BY ym) AS running
FROM rev ORDER BY ym;
MySQL vs SQLiteWindow syntax identical. Only date formatting differs: MySQL DATE_FORMAT(d,'%Y-%m') / YEAR()/MONTH() vs SQLite strftime('%Y-%m', d).

Essentials: ROW_NUMBER (unique 1,2,3), RANK (ties share, gaps), DENSE_RANK (ties share, no gaps), SUM() OVER(ORDER BY) (running total), LAG/LEAD (prev/next), PARTITION BY (restart per group).

💬 Interview — windows
  • RANK vs DENSE_RANK?
    a1,2,2,4 vs 1,2,2,3.
  • Top-N per group?
    aROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY g ORDER BY x DESC), keep rn≤N.
  • MoM growth?
    aLAG(rev) OVER(ORDER BY ym) then (rev−prev)/prev.
Where this shows up in real backend workWindow functions power 'rank within a group' features directly -- leaderboards, top-N-per-category listings, running totals on a dashboard. This is advanced SQL that shows up in real interview loops at data-heavy companies.

19 · Indexes + reading EXPLAIN

WhyNo index → read the whole table. An index (sorted B-tree) lets the DB jump to matches. The #1 lever for speed, and a guaranteed interview topic.
AnalogyNo index = reading a 900-page book cover-to-cover for a word. Index = the alphabetical index at the back — jump to the page.
🐬 MySQL 
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1234;
-- type: ALL = full scan
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust ON orders(customer_id);
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1234;
-- type: ref = index used
💜 Browser 
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1234;
-- SCAN orders
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust ON orders(customer_id);
-- then re-run → SEARCH ... USING INDEX
MySQL vs SQLiteMySQL EXPLAIN (read type: ALL=scan, ref/range=index) + EXPLAIN ANALYZE for timings. SQLite EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN (SCAN vs SEARCH USING INDEX). Creating indexes is identical.

▶ Prove it live — watch the plan flip (12,000-row table)

Trade-off: indexes slow writes & use disk. Index FKs and frequent WHERE/JOIN columns. A composite (a,b) helps a=? and a=? AND b=?, not b=? alone (left-to-right rule).
💬 Interview — indexes
  • Why not index everything?
    aWrites slow, storage grows. Index for read patterns.
  • Why an index gets ignored?
    aNon-SARGable: function on the column (YEAR(d)=2024), leading %, type mismatch.
Where this shows up in real backend workIndexes are the single biggest lever for query performance in a real production database -- knowing when EXPLAIN shows a full table scan versus an index seek is what separates a query that takes 2ms from one that takes 2 seconds at scale.

20 · Transactions

WhySome ops must be all-or-nothing (debit one account, credit another). A transaction guarantees both happen or neither.
ACID: Atomicity (all-or-nothing), Consistency (constraints hold), Isolation (concurrent txns don't corrupt), Durability (survives crash).
🐬 MySQL 
START TRANSACTION;
  UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-100 WHERE id=1;
  UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+100 WHERE id=2;
COMMIT;   -- or ROLLBACK; to undo BOTH
💜 Browser 
BEGIN;
  DELETE FROM txn_demo WHERE id=1;
ROLLBACK;  -- row comes back. Try below.
MySQL vs SQLiteMySQL START TRANSACTION, needs InnoDB. SQLite BEGIN. Both COMMIT/ROLLBACK. Locks preserve isolation (InnoDB = row locks; SQLite = brief whole-DB lock); the engine manages them.

▶ Delete then roll back

💬 Interview — transactions
  • ACID?
    aAtomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.
  • Deadlock?
    aTwo txns each hold a lock the other needs; engine kills one, app retries.
Where this shows up in real backend workTransactions are what keep a 'transfer $50 from account A to account B' operation from leaving the database half-updated if something fails midway -- this is the mechanism behind every payment or multi-step write in a real system.

21 · Performance basics

WhyCareless queries hang on big tables. Performance = removing the reasons the engine does extra work.
  1. Index what you filter/join on (biggest win).
  2. Keep predicates SARGable — compare the bare column:
    ❌ Index unusable
    WHERE YEAR(order_date)=2024
    ✅ Range, index-friendly
    WHERE order_date>='2024-01-01'
  AND order_date<'2025-01-01'
  3. Select only needed columns — avoid SELECT *.
  4. Filter early, aggregate late.
  5. Read the plan with EXPLAIN; don't guess.

▶ A real report query (revenue by category)

Where this shows up in real backend workQuery optimization is a real, recurring on-call task -- a slow query degrading under production load is one of the most common backend incidents, and this is the toolkit for diagnosing and fixing it.

24 · ⚑ Project B — Nimbus Retail (end to end)

Why one growing projectOne realistic system you designed, populated, reported on, and optimized beats ten toy tables. You've now taken Nimbus through the full lifecycle.
  1. Designed from requirements — 4 tables, a many-to-many bridge, 3NF.
  2. Created with constraints (PK/FK/NOT NULL/UNIQUE/CHECK).
  3. Populated ~30,000 rows (live in this page).
  4. Reported — revenue by category/month, top customers, running totals.
  5. Indexed & optimized — proved scan→index with EXPLAIN.
  6. Transaction-safe writes.
Capstone: build a real sales analytics dashboardFive staged, checked queries against the live Nimbus database (customers, products, orders, order_items) -- each one answers a real business question a stakeholder would actually ask. Each is graded against a live reference query on the SAME data you're querying, not a hardcoded number, so it's correct regardless of exactly how the ~30k rows were generated this session.

25 · 💼 Portfolio & interview kit

Skills to claim

Data modeling & normalization · constraints · multi-table joins · subqueries · CTEs · window functions · indexing & EXPLAIN-driven optimization · transactions/ACID · reporting on ~30k rows.

CV bullet (paste-ready)

Designed and built a normalized e-commerce database with enforced constraints; wrote analytical reports using CTEs and window functions, and improved query performance by adding indexes verified with EXPLAIN (full-scan → index-search).

Interview pitch (STAR)

S: learn SQL the industry way. T: design a realistic shop DB and answer business questions. A: modeled in 3NF with a bridge table, added constraints, seeded ~30k rows, wrote reports (monthly revenue + running totals, top customers), then EXPLAIN-profiled a slow lookup, added an FK index, confirmed scan→index-search. R: can design a schema and optimize queries, not just write SELECTs.

Questions they'll ask

  • Why quantity/price on order_items? → price at sale time belongs to the line.
  • Top 3 products per category? → ROW_NUMBER() PARTITION BY category, rn≤3.
  • Report got slow — diagnose? → EXPLAIN, find scans, index join/WHERE cols, SARGable predicates.
  • Save order + items together? → one transaction, COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

Interactive Python · in learning order

Don't just read Python.
Watch it run.

A real Python interpreter lives in this page. Write code and run it, or step through it line by line and watch every variable change. Then prove you've got it with exercises that check your answer automatically and tell you why it's wrong.

Python loads the first time you hit Run (~10s, once)

▶ Live interpreter

This is the real thing — CPython compiled to WebAssembly, running entirely in your browser. Nothing is sent anywhere. Change the code and run it.

scratch.py
Tip: press Tab to indent, and the editor keeps your indentation on Enter — so Python blocks stay lined up.

◉ Step visualizer — the signature feature

Why this changes everythingMost beginners lose the plot because code runs invisibly. Here you run it one line at a time and see exactly which line is executing and what every variable holds at that moment. Loops, function calls, and recursion stop being mysterious.
trace_me.py

Use ◀ / ▶ or the arrow keys to move through execution. The amber line is what's about to run; changed variables flash. The call-stack chips show which function you're inside — watch them pile up when you visualize recursion below.

print(), comments & variables

The mental modelprint() is how your program talks to you. A variable is a name tag you attach to a value so you can use it again later. A comment (starting with #) is ignored by Python entirely — it's a note to humans.
basics.py
Naming rule: variable names can use letters, numbers, and underscores, but can't start with a number. age2 is fine; 2age is not.
profile.py
Where this shows up in real backend workEvery backend service starts with variables holding config, request data, and state. The discipline of clear naming here is exactly what makes a production codebase navigable six months later, by someone who isn't you.

Data types & type conversion

The mental modelEvery value has a type: int (whole numbers), float (decimals), str (text), bool (True/False). Python figures out the type automatically, but sometimes you need to convert between them explicitly.
types.py
❌ Mixing types without converting
age = input("Age: ")
print(age + 1)
# TypeError: input() always
# returns a string
✅ Convert first
age = int(input("Age: "))
print(age + 1)
types2.py
Where this shows up in real backend workAPI payloads arrive as strings (JSON, form data, query params) and need explicit conversion before your business logic can use them safely -- this is the very first thing that goes wrong in a request handler if skipped.

input(), numbers & operators

The mental modelinput() pauses your program and waits for the person to type something — it always comes back as a str. Math operators (+ - * / // % **) work the way you'd expect, with two exceptions worth knowing: / always gives a float, and // floor-divides (drops the remainder).
operators.py
input() is commented out here since this page can't prompt for real keyboard input mid-script — but it works exactly like this in a normal Python file or terminal.
operators2.py
Where this shows up in real backend workPricing calculations, pagination math, rate-limit windows, retry backoff timers -- all of this is plain arithmetic, and the int/float and floor-division distinctions here are exactly where off-by-one and rounding bugs creep into billing code.

Strings: basics, methods, slicing & f-strings

The mental modelA string is text, but it's ALSO a sequence you can index and slice just like a list — "hello"[0] is 'h'. Strings come with dozens of built-in methods for common cleanup and transforms.
strings.py
strings2.py
Where this shows up in real backend workParsing log lines, sanitizing user input, building SQL/URL strings safely, formatting API responses -- string manipulation is a huge fraction of what backend code actually does day to day.

Booleans, comparisons & logical operators

The mental modelEvery comparison (== != < > <= >=) produces a bool: True or False. Combine booleans with and (both must be true), or (at least one), and not (flips it).
booleans.py
❌ = instead of ==
if age = 21:   # SyntaxError
    print("21!")
✅ == for comparing
if age == 21:   # = assigns,
    print("21!")   # == compares
booleans2.py
Where this shows up in real backend workEvery permission check, feature flag, and request-validation gate in a backend service is a boolean expression built from exactly these operators.

Conditionals: if / elif / else & ternary

The mental modelPython checks conditions top to bottom and runs the FIRST branch that's true, then skips the rest — even if a later condition would also be true. A ternary is a whole if/else squeezed onto one line, for simple cases.
conditionals.py
conditionals2.py
Where this shows up in real backend workRequest routing, permission checks, and validation logic are almost entirely if/elif/else chains -- getting the ordering and short-circuiting right is what keeps an API from leaking access it shouldn't.

Lists — a row of labelled boxes

Step 1 · Explanation
The mental modelA list is an ordered row of boxes, each with a number (its index) starting at 0. Everything about lists — indexing, slicing, appending — makes sense once you picture the boxes.
Step 2 · Guided example
Build a list live — append and pop, and watch the boxes and indices update:

Indexing reads a box; negative indexes count from the end; slicing takes a run of boxes (the end is exclusive):

lists.py
lists2.py
Step 7 · Mastery checkpoint
Where this shows up in real backend workQuery results, paginated API responses, and batch-processing pipelines are lists in Python. Understanding indexing and slicing cleanly is what keeps pagination code from off-by-one bugs.

Tuples & Sets

The mental modelA tuple is like a list that can't be changed after creation — use it for a fixed group of values (like coordinates). A set is an unordered bag with no duplicates — use it when you only care whether something is present, or need to remove duplicates fast.
tuples_sets.py
When to use which: list = ordered, changeable, duplicates OK. Tuple = ordered, fixed. Set = unordered, no duplicates, fast membership checks.
tuples2.py
Where this shows up in real backend workTuples show up as fixed API response shapes (status_code, body), and as dict/set keys when you need a compound key (e.g. (user_id, resource_id) for a permissions lookup). Sets are the backbone of deduplication and fast membership checks in request pipelines.

Dictionaries — labels, not positions

The mental modelA list finds things by position; a dictionary finds them by name (a key). Reach for a dict whenever "look this up by its id/word/name" describes what you need — it's near-instant no matter how big it gets.
Add key → value pairs and see the mapping:
The pattern that shows up everywhere — counting things with d.get(key, 0) + 1. .get returns a fallback (0) when the key isn't there yet, so you never crash on the first sighting. You'll use this in the word-frequency exercise.
dicts.py
dicts2.py
Where this shows up in real backend workJSON *is* nested dicts in Python. Every API request/response, every config file, every database row fetched as a mapping -- this is the data shape you'll touch most as a backend engineer.

References & mutability — the #1 source of bugs

Why it mattersIn Python a variable is a name tag on an object, not a box holding a copy. So b = a gives the same list two names. Change it through one name and the other "changes" too — because there's only one object. This trips up everyone; see it and you'll never lose an hour to it.
references.py
✗ Mutable default argument
def add(x, bag=[]):
    bag.append(x)
    return bag
# the list is shared across calls!
✓ Fresh each call
def add(x, bag=None):
    if bag is None:
        bag = []
    bag.append(x)
    return bag
references2.py
Where this shows up in real backend workPassing a mutable list or dict into a function and having a caller's data silently change is one of the most common real bugs in production Python -- this lesson is the single highest-value one in the whole course for that reason.
Step 1 · Explanation

Loops: for, range(), while, break & continue

The mental modelfor loops over a known sequence (a list, a string, a range()). while keeps going as long as a condition holds — use it when you don't know in advance how many times you'll loop. break exits the loop entirely; continue skips to the next iteration.
Step 2 · Guided example
loops.py
❌ Forgetting to update the loop variable
n = 3
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    # forgot n -= 1 -- runs forever!
✅ Always move toward the stopping condition
n = 3
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n -= 1
loops2.py
Step 7 · Mastery checkpoint
Where this shows up in real backend workProcessing batches of records, retrying failed API calls, paginating through a large result set -- almost all of it is a for or while loop, and knowing when to break/continue keeps that code from silently doing the wrong thing.

Functions: defining, parameters, return & scope

The mental modelA function packages up a piece of logic so you can reuse it by name instead of rewriting it. Parameters are the inputs; return sends a value back out. Variables created INSIDE a function only exist inside it — that's called scope.
functions.py
Keyword arguments (greeting="Hey") let you pass arguments by name, in any order — useful once a function has several parameters.
functions2.py
Where this shows up in real backend workA backend service is fundamentally hundreds of small functions calling each other -- route handlers calling service functions calling data-access functions. Clean parameter design here is what keeps that call chain maintainable.

Comprehensions — build a list from a sentence

The mental modelRead it left to right as English: [n*n for n in nums if n > 0] is "the square of n, for each n in nums, where n is positive." It's a loop that builds a list, compressed into one readable line.
comprehensions.py
When not to: if the logic needs more than one if or a nested condition that hurts to read, a plain loop is the better choice. Clever isn't the goal — clear is.
comprehensions2.py
Where this shows up in real backend workTransforming a database result set into an API response shape, or filtering a batch to just the records that need processing, is exactly what a comprehension does -- and it's the idiomatic way senior Python engineers write that kind of code.

Recursion — a function that calls itself

The mental modelEvery recursion needs two things: a base case that stops (or it runs forever), and a recursive case that moves toward the base. Picture a stack of unfinished calls waiting for the one beneath them to return.
AnalogyYou're in a cinema queue and want to know your row number. You can't see the front, so you ask the person ahead "what row are you in?" They ask the person ahead of them, and so on. The front-row person (the base case) answers "1"; each answer passes back +1 until it reaches you. That chain of waiting questions is the call stack.
recursion.py

Step through it and watch the fact chips stack up as each call waits, then unwind as each returns. That pile-and-unwind is recursion.

recursion2.py
Where this shows up in real backend workTraversing nested JSON, walking a permission tree, or processing a threaded comment structure are naturally recursive problems. Recursion also underlies how tree and graph algorithms work.

Errors & exceptions

The mental modelAn error that isn't handled crashes your program. try/except lets you catch a specific kind of error and decide what to do instead of crashing. raise lets you trigger your own error on purpose, with a message that explains what went wrong.
errors.py
Catch specific errors, not everything. except ZeroDivisionError tells you exactly what you handled; a bare except: hides bugs you didn't expect (see the Clean Code section below).
errors2.py
Where this shows up in real backend workProduction backend code is defined as much by its error handling as its happy path -- a payment API that doesn't handle a declined card gracefully, or a webhook handler that crashes on malformed input, is a real incident, not a bug ticket.

File handling

The mental modelopen() gives you a file object; with makes sure the file gets closed automatically, even if something goes wrong inside the block. This page can't touch your real filesystem, but the pattern below is exactly what you'd run locally.
files.py
This one actually works here — Pyodide gives your code a small virtual filesystem in the browser, so open()/write()/read() run for real. On your own machine, the exact same code reads and writes real files.
files2.py
Where this shows up in real backend workReading config files, writing logs, processing uploaded CSVs, generating reports -- file I/O with proper context managers (the 'with' pattern) is what keeps a service from leaking file handles under load.

Modules & imports

The mental modelA module is just a Python file full of functions someone already wrote. import brings it in so you can use it, instead of writing everything from scratch. Python ships with dozens of useful built-in modules.
modules.py
Two import styles: import math then math.sqrt(...), or from math import sqrt then just sqrt(...). The first is clearer about where a function came from.
modules2.py
Where this shows up in real backend workA real backend codebase is dozens or hundreds of files importing from each other -- this is the organizing principle of every non-trivial Python service you'll ever work in.

Lambda functions

The mental modelA lambda is a tiny, unnamed function written in one line — lambda x: x*2 is the same idea as def f(x): return x*2, just compact. They're mainly used where a function is expected as an argument, like sorted(..., key=...).
lambda.py
When NOT to use a lambda: if the logic needs more than one expression or a name would make it clearer, write a normal def function instead — a comprehension or named function almost always reads better than a complex lambda.
lambda2.py
Where this shows up in real backend worksorted()/filter()/map() with a lambda key shows up constantly in data-shaping code -- ranking search results, filtering a queryset, transforming a batch before writing it out.

*args & **kwargs — flexible arguments

The mental model*args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple; **kwargs collects extra named arguments into a dict. Use them when you don't know in advance how many arguments will come.
args.py
args2.py
Where this shows up in real backend workAPI client wrappers and decorators (logging, auth, retries) almost always use *args/**kwargs to stay generic across whatever function they're wrapping or calling -- it's the mechanism that makes middleware possible.

Generators — values on demand

The mental modelA normal function builds the whole list in memory and hands it back. A generator uses yield to hand back one value at a time, pausing in between — so it can produce huge or endless sequences using almost no memory.
AnalogyA list is a printed book — every page exists at once. A generator is a storyteller — you only get the next line when you ask, and they remember where they paused.
generators.py
generators2.py
Where this shows up in real backend workStreaming a large database export or API response without loading it all into memory at once is exactly what a generator is for -- this is a real memory/cost difference in production, not just an elegant trick.

Decorators — wrapping a function

The mental modelA decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a new one that adds behaviour around it — logging, timing, checking permissions — without touching the original's code. @name is just shorthand for "wrap this."
decorators.py
Decoded: @announce above add means add = announce(add). So calling add now runs wrapper, which prints, calls the real add, prints, and returns the result.
decorators2.py
Where this shows up in real backend workAuthentication checks, request logging, caching, and retry logic on API endpoints are almost always implemented as decorators in real backend frameworks (Flask, FastAPI, Django) -- this lesson is directly how that machinery works.

Classes & objects — your own data types

The mental modelA class is a blueprint; an object is a thing built from it. The blueprint says what data each thing carries (attributes) and what it can do (methods). self is "this particular object."
classes.py

Inheritance — building on an existing class

The mental modelA subclass inherits everything from a parent class, then can add or override behavior. Use it when one thing genuinely "is a" more specific version of another — a SavingsAccount IS A BankAccount, just with extra rules.
inheritance.py
super().__init__(...) calls the parent class's constructor so you don't have to repeat its setup logic — the subclass only writes what's genuinely new.
Where this shows up in real backend workDatabase models, service classes, and API client wrappers are classes. Inheritance specifically shows up in framework base classes you'll extend constantly (e.g. a base model class, a base API view class).

✦ Clean Python & common mistakes

Why botherWorking code and good code are different bars. Clean habits are what interviewers and teammates actually notice. Each pair below is a real trap and its fix.
✗ == vs is
if x is 5:      # unreliable
if name is "":  # unreliable
✓ Use == for values
if x == 5:
if name == ""
# 'is' is only for None / identity
✗ Bare except hides bugs
try:
    risky()
except:          # swallows everything
    pass
✓ Catch what you expect
try:
    risky()
except ValueError as e:
    print("bad value:", e)
✗ Mutating while looping
for x in items:
    if bad(x):
        items.remove(x)  # skips items
✓ Build a new list
items = [x for x in items
         if not bad(x)]
✗ Comparing floats exactly
if 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3:   # False!
✓ Compare with tolerance
import math
if math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3):
Naming: snake_case for variables and functions, UPPER_CASE for constants, CamelCase for classes. A good name (total_price) beats a comment explaining a bad one (tp).

✓ Exercises — write it, check it, understand it

How checking worksWrite your solution, hit Check, and it runs your code against hidden test cases in the real interpreter. If it's wrong, it shows you the exact input, what your code returned, and what was expected — so you learn from the gap, not just a red X.
A batch below is tagged "Real Assessment Practice" — longer, single-function problems (def solution(...)) written in the same style and difficulty as an actual internship coding assessment: a full worded description, worked examples with explanations, and explicit constraints, rather than a short docstring-style prompt.

🐞 Debugging challenges

WhyReading and fixing broken code is a different muscle than writing it from scratch — and it's most of real programming. Each snippet below has one bug. Find it, fix it, and Check.

▦ Projects

Why projectsExercises train single skills; projects make you combine them. Each one below has an auto-checked core function you build here, plus notes on turning it into the full real-world version on your own machine.
Mini · after strings

Slugify a title

Turn a title into a URL slug: lowercase, spaces → hyphens, and strip anything that isn't a letter, number, or hyphen. "Hello, World!" → "hello-world".

Mini · after dicts

Tally a vote

Given a list of vote strings, return a dict of each option to its count, and build toward reporting the winner.

Real-world · data processing

Parse & summarize records

Given a list of "name,score" strings (like rows from a CSV), return the average score. This is the core of every data-cleaning script.

Turn this into the full script locally

On your own machine the same logic reads a real file: open("scores.csv"), loop the lines, line.strip().split(","), and aggregate. In this page there's no file system, so you build and test the pure logic here, then drop it into a main() that opens the file. That separation — testable logic vs I/O — is exactly how professionals structure scripts.

Real-world · CLI app core

To-do list operations

Build the core operation a CLI to-do app needs: given a list of tasks and a command, return the updated list. Here: toggle_done(tasks, i) flips the "done" flag of task i.

Turn this into the full CLI locally

Wrap this logic in a while True: loop that reads input() commands ("add", "done 2", "list", "quit") and prints the list each time. Save/load with json.dump/json.load. The operation you built here is the tested heart; the loop and file I/O are the shell around it.

Roadmap · Step 5 · in learning order

Object-Oriented
Programming.

Model real systems with classes. Five lessons — classes & objects, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, and composition — each with a runnable example and auto-checked practice, on the same real Python interpreter as the Python track.

Shares the Python engine — loads on first Run (~10s, once)

Classes & Objects

The mental modelA class is a blueprint; an object is a thing built from it. The class says "a Dog has a name and an age and can bark"; each object is one specific dog with its own values. __init__ runs when you build one, and self is how an object refers to its own data.
oop-classes.py
Every object carries its own copy of the data. d1 and d2 are both Dogs, but changing one never touches the other.

Encapsulation

The mental modelEncapsulation means an object hides its internals and only exposes safe methods. Callers use account.deposit(10) — they never reach in and set the balance directly. By convention, a leading underscore (self._balance) marks something "internal, hands off." This lets the object protect its own rules.
oop-encapsulation.py
Because every change goes through deposit(), the object can reject invalid input. If callers could write a._balance = -999 directly, that protection would vanish.

Inheritance

The mental modelInheritance lets a class reuse another class's code. A Dog is an Animal, so it inherits everything Animal has and overrides only what differs. super().__init__(...) runs the parent's setup so you don't rewrite it.
oop-inheritance.py
describe() is written once in Animal, yet each subclass produces different output — because self.speak() resolves to the actual object's version.

Polymorphism

The mental modelPolymorphism means "same call, different behavior." If every shape has an area() method, you can loop a mixed list of shapes and call .area() on each — without checking its type. Add a new shape later and the loop needs zero changes. Dunder methods (__add__, __eq__) plug your objects into Python's own operators.
oop-polymorphism.py
sum(...) doesn't know or care which shapes it's holding. That's the power: code written against a shared interface (.area()) works for types that don't exist yet.

Composition over Inheritance

The mental modelNot every relationship is "is-a." A Car isn't a kind of Engine — it has one. Composition builds objects by holding other objects as attributes. It's often more flexible than inheritance: swap the Engine for a different one without touching the rest of the Car.
oop-composition.py
"Favor composition over inheritance" is one of the most repeated pieces of design advice — assembling objects from parts keeps them flexible and avoids deep, rigid class hierarchies.
